explanations.answer: They proclaim the resurrection in Jesus
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The text says the leaders were “…greatly disturbed that they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead.” (Acts 4:2) So the message was the trouble, and it brought the priests, the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees right up to Peter and John.

Nope, nothing in this passage says a word about offerings. The text says the leaders were disturbed that Peter and John were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead (Acts 4:2). So what disturbed them was the message, not money.

explanations.answer: They break the Sabbath in the temple
explanations.explanation: The Sabbath never comes up in this passage. What bothered the priests, the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees was that Peter and John were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead (Acts 4:2). The message itself was the problem. I'd have loved an easier thing to explain, but that's what the text says.
Five thousand, baker! The text says “…the number of men grew to about five thousand.” (Acts 4:4) It also says many who heard the message believed. That's a whole lot of believers, friend.

Close, but that number belongs to a different day. About three thousand were added to the believers back on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:41). Here the text says the number of men grew to about five thousand (Acts 4:4). Same kind of good news, bigger crowd.

You're short a zero there, friend. The text says the number of men grew to about five thousand (Acts 4:4). That's ten times what you picked. I know a thing or two about missing a zero, and I'm not proud of my math either.

explanations.answer: By what power or name they did it
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The leaders question them: “By what power or what name did you do this?” (Acts 4:7) They want to know who is behind the healing. I think Peter was glad they asked, because he had a very good answer.

explanations.answer: Why they healed on the Sabbath day
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention the Sabbath anywhere in this scene. The leaders ask, “By what power or what name did you do this?” (Acts 4:7) They're asking about the source of the healing. Nothing about the calendar.

explanations.answer: If the man was truly lame before
explanations.explanation: Nobody asks that, friend. The leaders ask, “By what power or what name did you do this?” (Acts 4:7) They later admit “…a remarkable miracle has occurred through them, and we cannot deny it.” (Acts 4:16) The question was never whether it happened, only who was behind it.

Right on the money, friend. Peter says, “It is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead, that this man stands before you healed.” (Acts 4:10) He's not hiding the name or mumbling it. He says it plainly, in front of the very leaders who asked.

Elijah was a great prophet of Israel (1 Kings 17:1), but Peter never mentions him here. Peter says the man stands healed by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth (Acts 4:10). The name he gives is the one he's been standing on all along.

Moses, Israel's leader, doesn't come up in Peter's answer. Peter says it's “…by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth…” that the man stands there healed (Acts 4:10). Peter had one name on his lips, and it wasn't Moses.

That's not what Peter does. He tells them, “…Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead…” (Acts 4:10). There's no softening in that line at all. I've seen people dodge a hard truth for a whole afternoon, and Peter does the opposite.

False is right, baker. Peter says Jesus is the one “…whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead…” (Acts 4:10) He puts it straight to the council and doesn't tiptoe around it. And he doesn't stop at the crucifixion, because God raised Jesus up.

explanations.answer: The rulers and elders in that room
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Peter is talking to “Rulers and elders of the people!” (Acts 4:8) and then says Jesus is “the stone you builders rejected…” (Acts 4:11) He says “you,” and the rulers and elders are the ones he's speaking to. Peter's not shy, that's for sure.

Peter isn't talking to soldiers here. He's speaking to the rulers and elders of the people (Acts 4:8), and he says Jesus is “the stone you builders rejected…” (Acts 4:11) The “you” points at the people in front of him, not at Rome's soldiers.

The nations far away aren't the ones Peter is talking to, friend. Peter is speaking to “Rulers and elders of the people!” (Acts 4:8) Then he says Jesus is “the stone you builders rejected…” (Acts 4:11) That “you” is aimed at the ones he's speaking to.

Name, that's the word. Peter says, “Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.” (Acts 4:12) He's already been talking about the name of Jesus, and now he says it's the only one. That's a big statement from a man who was in custody the night before.

Law is a fair guess, but it's not the word Peter uses. He says there is “…no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.” (Acts 4:12) He keeps coming back to the name of Jesus, from the question the leaders asked to the answer he gave.

The temple isn't the word in this verse, friend. Peter says, “…there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.” (Acts 4:12) Salvation is tied to a name, and that name is Jesus.

Jesus it is, baker. The council saw their boldness, realized they were unschooled, ordinary men, “…they marveled and took note that these men had been with Jesus.” (Acts 4:13) The council could see it, and the text doesn't say it was anything else. Being around Jesus leaves a mark.

Gamaliel was a Pharisee and a teacher of the law (Acts 5:34), but he's not the name in this verse. The council took note that Peter and John “…had been with Jesus.” (Acts 4:13) That's the name the verse gives.

Herod does show up later in this passage, but not here. The believers name him as one who conspired against Jesus (Acts 4:27). What the council took note of in verse 13 was that these men “…had been with Jesus.”

True, friend. The text says that “…seeing the man who had been healed standing there with them, they had nothing to say in response.” (Acts 4:14) The healed man was right there with them. That's the kind of moment where you open your mouth and nothing comes out.

The text says the opposite. “And seeing the man who had been healed standing there with them, they had nothing to say in response.” (Acts 4:14) So the council was quiet, and the healed man was on his feet. When a thing is that plain, there's not much left to say.

explanations.answer: Warn them not to speak in this name
explanations.explanation: That's what they decide, baker. They say, “…to keep this message from spreading any further among the people, we must warn them not to speak to anyone in this name.” (Acts 4:17) They can't deny the miracle, so they go after the message instead.

explanations.answer: Run them out of Jerusalem for good
explanations.explanation: They never talk about running anyone out of the city. Their plan is that “…we must warn them not to speak to anyone in this name.” (Acts 4:17) It's a warning, not a banishment.

explanations.answer: Hand them over to Pilate for trial
explanations.explanation: Pilate isn't part of this plan. The council says, “…we must warn them not to speak to anyone in this name.” (Acts 4:17) Their answer is a warning, and that's all the text gives.

explanations.answer: Speaking about what they saw and heard
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Peter and John say, “For we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard.” (Acts 4:20) They saw it and heard it, and they can't keep it in. I couldn't keep quiet about a fresh batch of cookies, either.

explanations.answer: Healing everyone who asks them to
explanations.explanation: That's not what they say. Peter and John answer, “For we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard.” (Acts 4:20) Their words are about speaking, not about taking requests.

explanations.answer: Traveling from one town to the next
explanations.explanation: Traveling doesn't come up in their answer. They say, “For we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard.” (Acts 4:20) What they can't stop is speaking, not traveling.

Glorifying, baker! The text says, “They could not find a way to punish them, because all the people were glorifying God for what had happened.” (Acts 4:21) The whole crowd was praising God. The council had a problem, and the crowd was the reason.
It's the other way around, friend. The text says “…all the people were glorifying God for what had happened.” (Acts 4:21) That's why the council couldn't find a way to punish Peter and John.
Doubt isn't the word in this verse. The text says “…all the people were glorifying God for what had happened.” (Acts 4:21) A crowd that's praising God makes it hard for a council to punish anybody.

True, baker. The text says, “When the believers heard this, they lifted up their voices to God with one accord.” (Acts 4:24) They lifted their voices together. The report came from Peter and John, who had returned to their own people (Acts 4:23).

The text says otherwise. “When the believers heard this, they lifted up their voices to God with one accord.” (Acts 4:24) So they prayed, and they prayed together. I think I'd have needed a minute before I got that far.

explanations.answer: The Lord and His Anointed One
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The believers quote David, “The kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together against the Lord and against His Anointed One.” (Acts 4:26) They're gathering against the Lord Himself and His Anointed One.
The prophets and priests aren't who the psalm names. David's words say the rulers gather “…against the Lord and against His Anointed One.” (Acts 4:26) Those are the two it points to.

explanations.answer: The temple and the holy city
explanations.explanation: The psalm doesn't say that. It says the kings and rulers gather together “…against the Lord and against His Anointed One.” (Acts 4:26) Those are the two it names, not a building or a city.

Yes, baker. The believers pray, “They carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen.” (Acts 4:28) They were plotting, but what they ended up carrying out is what God's hand and will had decided beforehand. The believers say it right in their prayer.

explanations.answer: A warning given in a dream
explanations.explanation: No dream is mentioned in the prayer. The believers say Herod and Pilate “…carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen.” (Acts 4:28) What they carried out was what God had decided beforehand.

explanations.answer: Orders sent to them from Rome
explanations.explanation: Rome isn't in this verse. The believers pray that they “…carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen.” (Acts 4:28) The prayer points to what God's hand and will had decided, and that's the only source it names.

Boldness is right, baker. They pray, “…enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness…” (Acts 4:29) They'd just brought their council's threats before God, and they asked for complete boldness. I'd have asked for a different problem.

That's not what they ask for. After “…consider their threats…” the prayer says, “…enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness…” (Acts 4:29) Their request is about speaking God's word.

Judgment on their enemies isn't in the prayer. They say, “…consider their threats, and enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness…” (Acts 4:29) What they ask is for God to enable them to speak His word with complete boldness.
Shaken, baker! The text says, “After they had prayed, their meeting place was shaken…” (Acts 4:31) The place was shaken after the prayer. That's one memorable prayer meeting.
There's no flood in this passage. The text says, “After they had prayed, their meeting place was shaken…” (Acts 4:31) The place shook, and nothing was said about water.
The text doesn't say it went dark. It says, “After they had prayed, their meeting place was shaken…” (Acts 4:31) Shaken is the word, friend.

The text says the opposite, friend. After the shaking, “…they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God boldly.” (Acts 4:31) They spoke boldly, right after asking for exactly that.

False is right, baker. “…they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God boldly.” (Acts 4:31) They had just asked for boldness, and the text says they spoke boldly. The same council that threatened them had no say in that.
